title: Databases
whyItMatters: Enough to reason about why a screen is slow and what your API is really costing the server.

questions.prompt: What does adding an index cost you?
options: Nothing — it only speeds things up
Storage, and slower writes, since every insert must update it
Read consistency across transactions
The ability to query the column directly
questions.explanation: An index is a second sorted structure the database must keep in step, so every write pays for it.

concept.title: An index is a second copy
concept.summary: Reads get faster because writes do more work.
points: A B-tree index keeps the column sorted for fast lookup and range scans.
Every insert, update and delete must maintain every index on the table.
Unused indexes are pure cost — they slow writes and buy nothing.
Write-heavy tables are where over-indexing hurts most.

questions.prompt: An endpoint returns 100 posts and issues 101 queries. What is happening?
options: The connection pool is too small
Each post's author is fetched in its own query after the list query
The query is missing an index
The ORM is retrying failed queries
questions.explanation: One query for the list plus one per row is the N+1 pattern — usually a lazily-loaded relation inside a loop.

concept.title: N+1 queries
concept.summary: The count gives it away: rows + 1.
points: One query loads the list; touching a relation per row fires another each time.
Latency multiplies even though each query looks fast in isolation.
Fix by joining or by batching the second query with an IN clause.
Prisma's `include`, SQL's JOIN and DataLoader all solve the same problem.

questions.prompt: A column is indexed but the query still does a full scan. Which of these explains it?
options: The query returns more than one row
The query wraps the column in a function, such as LOWER(email)
The table has fewer than a million rows
The index was created after the rows were inserted
questions.explanation: A plain index on the original column may not support a predicate on a transformed value such as LOWER(email). Depending on the database, an expression index or a rewritten predicate can make that access path available; EXPLAIN shows what the optimizer actually chose.

concept.title: When an index goes unused
concept.summary: Usually the query, not the index, is the problem.
points: A transformed predicate may not use a plain column index; an expression index can support the transformed value.
A composite index only helps if the query uses its leading column.
A leading wildcard, LIKE '%term', cannot use a B-tree.
EXPLAIN tells you what the planner actually chose. Read it.

questions.prompt: Two updates run inside one transaction. The second fails and the transaction is rolled back. What is the durable result?
options: The first is kept and the second is retried
Both are rolled back, as if neither happened
The first is kept and the transaction stays open
The database decides based on isolation level
questions.explanation: After rollback, atomicity makes the transaction's writes all-or-nothing, so neither update is committed. A statement error does not have identical automatic behavior in every database or client; the application or database still has to roll the transaction back rather than commit partial work.

concept.title: ACID, briefly
concept.summary: Four guarantees, and they answer different questions.
points: Atomicity: all of it or none of it.
Consistency: constraints hold before and after.
Isolation: how much concurrent transactions can see of each other.
Durability: once committed, it survives a crash.

questions.prompt: Read Committed prevents which of these?
options: Reading a value another transaction has written but not committed
Getting a different result from the same query twice in one transaction
New rows appearing in a repeated range query
All of the above
questions.explanation: In the SQL isolation model, Read Committed rules out dirty reads but allows a later statement to observe committed changes, including non-repeatable reads and phantoms. Exact guarantees at stronger named levels vary by database implementation, so production decisions must use that database's documentation.

concept.title: What each level rules out
concept.summary: Stricter levels cost concurrency, so pick the weakest that is correct.
points: Read Uncommitted: dirty reads allowed.
Read Committed: no dirty reads; the same query can still change.
SQL-standard Repeatable Read disallows non-repeatable reads but may allow phantoms; some databases provide stronger snapshot behavior.
Serializable: as if transactions ran one at a time.

questions.prompt: A query is instant on your laptop and slow in production. What differs?
expects: names data volume or distribution as the main difference
mentions the planner choosing differently at scale
reaches for EXPLAIN or real measurement
questions.probeIfMissing: How many rows does your local database have compared to production?

concept.title: Why local lies
concept.summary: The plan that is fast on a thousand rows can be quadratic on ten million.
points: A full scan is cheap on a small table, so a missing index never shows up locally.
Planners use table statistics, and yours are nothing like production's.
Concurrency, locks and cold caches only exist under real load.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE against production-shaped data is the only honest test.

questions.prompt: A list endpoint got slower every week for a month with no code changes. What is your first move?
expects: connects the gradual slowdown to growing data
proposes a measurement before a fix
names a plausible cause such as a missing index, a full scan or unbounded pagination
questions.probeIfMissing: What changes week over week if the code does not?

concept.title: Slow growth means data growth
concept.summary: A gradual curve almost always tracks row count.
points: No deploy plus steady decay points at the table, not the code.
A query with no LIMIT returns more every week by definition.
A full scan degrades linearly; an index keeps it near flat.
Check row counts and EXPLAIN before touching anything.

questions.prompt: Someone proposes indexing every column that appears in a WHERE clause. What is wrong with that?
expects: names the write cost of maintaining each index
distinguishes indexes that are actually used from ones that are not
questions.probeIfMissing: What has to happen on every insert once a table has ten indexes?

concept.title: Indexes are not free
concept.summary: Each one is another structure to keep in step on every write.
points: Every insert, update and delete maintains every index on the table.
Indexes compete for the same buffer cache as your data.
A composite index often replaces several single-column ones.
Databases expose index usage stats — drop the ones nothing reads.

questions.prompt: Users occasionally end up with two identical orders. Where do you start?
expects: considers a double submit, a retry, or a race between two requests
reaches for a uniqueness guarantee rather than only a UI fix
distinguishes preventing it from detecting it
questions.probeIfMissing: What does the client do when the request times out but the server already committed?

concept.title: Duplicates are a concurrency bug
concept.summary: A disabled button narrows the window; it does not close it.
points: A retry after a timeout submits a request the server may already have run.
Two concurrent requests can both pass a check-then-insert.
A unique constraint is the only guarantee the database will enforce.
An idempotency key lets the retry return the original result instead of failing.
